extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public opinion, journalists, commentators, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and heuristics for recognizing, analysing, and judging stereotypes and moral/ideological 'codes' that shape public opinion; aimed at improving critical judgment about how facts are perceived and used in public discourse. Emphasises detection of blind spots, practical constraints, contradictions, and the factual assumptions embedded in codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes create blind spots
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes simplify and fix our images of how things behave and thereby produce blind spots where relevant facts are censored out of attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that a point exists where 'the blind spots come from the edge of vision into the center.' When a stereotype is uncritically held it 'not only censors out much that needs to be taken into account, but when the day of reckoning comes... that which it did wisely take into account is ship-wrecked with it.' Example: postwar complacency and the misreading of political/economic realities after 1919–1921. Anti-pattern: assuming a stereotype is a full account rather than a simplifying device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh the utility versus distortion of stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes economize effort and preserve energy by excluding distracting images, but this saving has costs when important contrary facts are suppressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the stereotype's time-saving or motivational function as neither wholly good nor wholly bad: note its function ('saves time in a busy life', 'defense of our position') and simultaneously test whether it omits disturbing facts. Example: progressive stereotype inciting work while obscuring decisions about what work to do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify spots of 'blind automatism' in theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Every grand theory contains a locus where it assumes automatic processes (automatism) that conceal facts which, if considered, would check the theory's movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask what fact is being covered by the automatism (e.g., laissez-faire assumes spontaneous harmony; collectivism assumes bureaucratic efficiency; imperialism assumes governors know governed needs). If you find an assumed automatic mechanism, probe for suppressed countervailing facts and the practical consequences of those assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertness measured by multiplicity of aspects and discounting expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: True expertise is the multiplication of aspects one is prepared to discover, plus the habit of discounting one's expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate experts not by confidence but by the range of distinct aspects they consider and their willingness to temper preconceptions. Anti-pattern: narrow 'expertness' that forces all phenomena into a single stereotype (e.g., cavalry experts poor at trench/tank warfare).

rubrics_metrics.name: Codes embed factual assumptions and must be examined as hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral, legal, economic, professional, and patriotic 'codes' rest on specific pictures of human nature, institutions, and history; in scientific codes these are treated as hypotheses, in mythic codes they are accepted without question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a code, make explicit the underlying map of facts (psychology, sociology, history). Test whether the code treats these assumptions as provisional (scientific) or as completed myth (dogmatic). Example: economic maxims assume specific economic motives; patriotic codes assume different motives in war. Consequence: codes that don't treat assumptions as hypotheses lack the critical means to separate truth from error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare codes by reexamining the underlying visions of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Useful discussion should reexamine visions of facts rather than merely compare moral ideals, because codes primarily determine which facts are observed and how they are judged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When two sides disagree, ask whether they simply have different factual patterns (stereotypes) and make those patterns explicit. Example: capitalist vs socialist patterns produce different perceptions of the same events; resolving disputes requires interrogating the factual maps, not merely moral rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect contradictions among invoked principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A rapid series of contradictory absolute principles used to justify different claims is a clue that stereotypes, not consistent reason, are being used to censor out troublesome facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for mutually incompatible principles invoked across different sectors of an argument (e.g., historic right, geographic frontier, cultural superiority, reparation, defense) — this pattern often reveals constructed propaganda rather than principled logic (Ruritania example). Contradiction is a diagnostic for false absolutism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for inability to account for space and practical constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments or policies that treat geographic distance, transport, logistics, or other practical constraints as negligible reveal stereotyped thinking that ignores material facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask how resources, transport, time, and routes affect the feasibility of proposals (e.g., the demand to 'reestablish an Eastern Front' ignoring 5,000 miles and broken railways; projecting armies 'on a magic carpet'). If spatial/practical facts are mentally 'compressed' or absent, downgrade credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for absolutist principles that censor context
rubrics_metrics.description: When someone argues from an absolute, eternal principle (e.g., 'self-determination' or 'natural right') and treats particular cases as perfect exemplars, that principle censors context and background and tends to convert argument into fight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question whether invoking an 'eternal principle' is obscuring real particulars (fact, context, human costs). If so, demand concrete particulars rather than abstract rhetoric. The text warns that moving to absolute principles provokes escalating defenses and hampers accommodation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to projection and 'reading back' of stereotypes into biographies
rubrics_metrics.description: People tend to read the stereotypes' assumed qualities back into successful individuals or events, thereby mistaking a constructed model for an accurate account of how success actually occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading biographies or official accounts, separate the model's assumptions (e.g., capitalist saved capital, entrepreneur organized factory) from the messy actual sequence of events. Anticipate confirmation bias: success is used to validate the stereotype rather than the reverse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify emotional loading of stereotypes (prejudice, sentiment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes are suffused with preference, affection, dislike and strong sentiments; these emotional attachments shape perception and moral judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note language and affect (e.g., 'blushing maiden', 'wily Oriental') and test whether emotional valence determines what facts are noticed. Where prejudice is present, evaluate the possibility that perception is being shaped to confirm sentiment rather than evidence. Recommendation: detect, discount, and refine prejudices rather than eliminate them (impractical ideal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish mythic codes from those open to scientific testing
rubrics_metrics.description: A myth treats truth and error, fact and fancy as on the same plane and resists criteria that could separate them; scientific-influenced codes treat their conceptions as hypotheses requiring proof or contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the code's central assumptions are open to evidence-based testing. If not, the code will be 'dogmatic' and impervious to corrective facts; if yes, prioritize evidence and revise accordingly. Example: contrast mythic acceptance of a code versus moralists who accept scientific discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of conspiracy narratives as explanations for opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Labeling opponents or social phenomena as the product of hidden plots (profiters, capitalist plots, Bolshevik gold, spies) is often a stereotype used to explain complex social phenomena away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat conspiratorial explanations as a heuristic of last resort; seek fuller causal accounts (institutional, economic, social) before adopting a conspiracy framing. The text catalogs how many issues (price rises, strikes, elections) are rendered into 'plots' by stereotype-driven thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether a code's applicability conditions are present
rubrics_metrics.description: Every code applies to certain typical situations; one must judge whether the present predicament matches the situation the code had in mind (e.g., self-defence exceptions to 'Thou shalt not kill').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand interpretation and secondary rules: around every code there is 'a cloud of interpreters' who deduce particulars. Evaluate the legitimacy and accuracy of those interpretations; check whether facts have been misjudged or provisions misapplied (provocation vs self-defence example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster critical education that recognizes opinions as partial
rubrics_metrics.description: Tolerance and better judgement arise when people habitually recognize their opinions as partial experiences filtered by stereotypes rather than as total, absolute realities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote habits of seeing opinions as 'a partial experience seen through our stereotypes.' Encourage practices that make one's own factual maps explicit and open to challenge; this counters the instinct to brand opponents as dishonest or absurd when disagreement may stem from different perceived facts.
